options: A Salesforce-specific authentication service
A general-purpose API client application used to build, test, and share HTTP request collections
A Salesforce API resource for querying metadata
A SOAP-only testing tool that cannot send REST requests
questions.explain: Postman is not a Salesforce product at all — it's a general-purpose tool for sending and organizing HTTP requests against any API.

questions.q: What problem do Postman environment variables (like {{access_token}}) solve?
options: They let you avoid hardcoding values like an instance URL or access token into every saved request, so updating one variable updates every request that references it
They encrypt the request body automatically
They are required by Salesforce's REST API to process any request
They replace the need for an Authorization header entirely
questions.explain: Environment variables centralize values that change often (like an expiring access token) so you update them in one place instead of across every saved request.

questions.q: How does Postman's Authorization tab help when sending a Bearer-token-authenticated request?
options: It formats and adds the Authorization: Bearer ... header for you once you select Bearer Token and supply the value
It automatically obtains a new OAuth token without any user input, bypassing all flows
It converts the request into a SOAP request
It is only usable with the legacy Username-Password flow
questions.explain: Selecting Bearer Token as the auth type and providing the token value lets Postman construct the correct Authorization header automatically, rather than typing it by hand.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does it organize an example Postman collection into folders like Auth, Accounts, Queries, and Limits?
options: Because Salesforce requires that exact folder structure
To mirror the API's resources, making the collection easy to navigate and hand off to someone else later
Because each folder represents a different OAuth flow
Folders are required for a collection to run at all
questions.explain: Grouping requests by resource, with the HTTP verb visible in each request's name, is purely an organizational practice that makes a collection maintainable over time.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe Postman's concepts in plain text rather than with screenshots?
options: Because this course's screenshot policy for this code-only course teaches through real HTTP/JSON examples, referencing tools like Postman by name only
Because Postman has no visual interface at all
Because screenshots of Postman are copyrighted and cannot be described in any form
Because Postman is being deprecated by Salesforce
questions.explain: This course is code-only and conceptual — Postman is referenced by name as a tool you'd use, but the actual teaching happens through the HTTP requests themselves, which apply regardless of which client sends them.
